questions.question: A request has a valid, unexpired JWT — but the user's role doesn't match what an endpoint requires. What status code should it get?
questions.explanation: 401 means 'we don't know who you are' (missing/invalid token). 403 means 'we know who you are, and you're not allowed to do this' — the correct response when a valid but insufficiently-privileged token is presented.

questions.question: What's the benefit of a named policy (`AddPolicy("AdminOnly", ...)`) over repeating `policy.RequireRole("Admin")` on every endpoint?
options: Named policies are faster at runtime
Define the rule once, reuse it by name everywhere — avoids repeating (and risking inconsistency in) the same authorization logic
Named policies are required by ASP.NET Core
questions.explanation: This is the DRY principle (Module 1) applied to authorization rules — define once, reference by name, and a future change to what 'AdminOnly' means only needs to happen in one place.

questions.question: What does CORS actually restrict?
options: All access to your API from any client, browser or not
Which origins (websites) a BROWSER will allow to call your API via JavaScript — it doesn't restrict HttpClient, curl, Postman, or other non-browser clients
Which HTTP methods your API supports
questions.explanation: CORS is a browser-enforced same-origin policy relaxation mechanism. It has no effect on requests made outside a browser context (HttpClient, curl, server-to-server calls) — those were never blocked by the same-origin policy to begin with.

questions.question: What does `.WithOrigins("https://myfrontend.com").AllowAnyHeader().AllowAnyMethod()` configure?
options: That browser JavaScript running on https://myfrontend.com is allowed to call this API, with any headers and any HTTP method
That the API only accepts requests from a specific IP address
questions.explanation: This is a CORS policy: it names an allowed origin and what that origin's browser-based requests are permitted to include.

questions.question: Skipping CORS configuration entirely prevents any unauthorized access to your API.
questions.explanation: CORS only affects browser-based JavaScript calls from other origins — it is NOT a general access control mechanism. An API without CORS configured is still fully reachable by HttpClient, curl, Postman, or a browser simply navigating directly to it. Authentication/authorization (this module) is what actually restricts access; CORS is about controlling cross-origin BROWSER behavior.

questions.question: Middleware order matters for `app.UseCors(...)`, just as it does for authentication and authorization.
questions.explanation: Like every middleware (lesson 01), UseCors must be positioned correctly in the pipeline — typically early, before the request reaches routing/authorization — for cross-origin requests (including preflight OPTIONS requests) to be handled correctly.
